extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, administrative law practitioners, tribunal administrators, and students studying Canadian social security/pension appeals
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly/legal analysis of the constitutional, legislative and jurisprudential context governing the Pension Appeals Board (PAB) and its appellate/administrative procedures under the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. Focuses on jurisdictional allocation, statutory/regulatory sources, procedural rules, and practical implications for review and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three legal factors determining PAB activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Three factors determine and influence the PAB's activity in the strictly legal sense: the Constitution, legislation (together with its accompanying regulations), and the jurisprudence of the regular courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper analysis of the PAB must address all three dimensions: constitutional allocation of power, the statutory and regulatory framework that actually governs the Board's organization/jurisdiction/procedure, and relevant judicial decisions that have specified the nature and limits of the institutions created by those laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional division of legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional basis for provincial jurisdiction in social security matters rests on provisions such as the BNA Act grant: 'The establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals.' Subsections (13) and (16) of s.92 were the practical means originally relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any evaluation must identify which aspects of social security fall within provincial 'property and civil rights' or local matters (s.92(13), s.92(16)) and how the nineteenth-century wording has been used to found provincial authority over modern social security measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical legislative development and judicial interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative initiatives (e.g., work-accident compensation, allowances to needy mothers, unemployment insurance in 1935) and judicial responses (Supreme Court and Privy Council rulings) shaped whether federal or provincial authority was recognized — e.g., the 1935 unemployment insurance statute was struck down as beyond federal power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal analysis should trace relevant historical statutes and key judicial decisions because they determine present jurisdictional boundaries and explain why later constitutional amendments or federal-provincial arrangements were pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional amendments and arrangements as jurisdictional tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government obtained constitutional amendments (e.g., insertion under s.91 a new subsection (2A) for unemployment insurance in 1940 and section 94A in 1951 for old-age pensions) and requested further amendments to extend concurrent jurisdiction to 'additional benefits' including survivors and disabled persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing PAB authority or possible federal initiatives, account for amendments (their scope and reservations) and the fact that some federal interventions were authorized only through express constitutional change or by provincial consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effect of federal residual and spending powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The division of powers is made considerably more flexible through the residual jurisdiction and 'spending power' vested in the federal Parliament; combined with fiscal imbalances this has created a broad federal-provincial sector in social security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where formal legislative authority is provincial, the federal role via spending/financing often determines conception and practical realization of social security programmes; analyses must consider fiscal instruments and spending power as de facto determinants of policy and design.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB's dual/jurisdictional character ('double personality')
rubrics_metrics.description: Although created by federal law, the PAB exercises additional jurisdiction by special mandate of a provincial legislature and thus 'acts as a federal administrative authority on some occasions and as a provincial administrative authority on others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For any PAB decision, it is necessary to establish under which jurisdiction (federal or provincial) the agency acted because that determines the applicable law, procedure, and the proper court for judicial review (Federal Court or the provincial Superior Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory provisions that define PAB rights, scope and procedure (CPP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the Canada Pension Plan, sections relevant to the PAB include: s.29 (establishes the right of appeal to the PAB, mode of introducing the appeal, scope of decision-making power, reference to s.85), s.30 (enumerates issues, authoritativeness of decisions, right to appeal to the Supreme Court), s.37 (removes appeals regarding self‑employed earnings), and in Part II s.85–88 (establish right of appeal re benefits; composition, powers, areas of review, modification of decisions, compensation and costs); s.91(1)(c) empowers Governor General in Council to regulate procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any evaluation of PAB jurisdiction, procedure or remedies must cite and apply these specific statutory provisions and note their particular effects (e.g., limits on jurisdiction, appeal routes, procedural rule‑making power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations and procedural instruments govern appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal body of regulatory provisions is the Canada Pension Plan Regulations which specify substantive points of the CPP and administrative procedure. Separate statutory instruments adopted under s.41 and s.91 govern appeals lodged with the PAB (contributions) and procedural rules for the Review Committee and the PAB (benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the multiple layers of procedural regulation: initial administrative decision, prescribed review levels (e.g., Review Committee), and the PAB as the final administrative appellate body; examine the relevant Parts and Sections of the Regulations (e.g., Parts I, II for contributions; Part V for benefits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive form of agency statute does not determine autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal legislative practice varies (some agencies created by dedicated Acts; others by provisions included in broader Acts) and 'no discernible connection exists between the essential characteristics of a given autonomous administrative agency and the form of the legislative text that created it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer the degree of an agency's autonomy merely from whether it was created by a standalone statute or embedded in a larger Act; assess autonomy using substantive criteria and practice rather than statutory form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quebec Pension Plan: structure and procedural distinctions affecting PAB jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The QPP contains seven Titles (Definitions and application; Quebec Pension Board; Contributions; Benefits; Review; Administration; Final provisions). Title Five (Review) provides distinct avenues of recourse for contributions and benefits (e.g., appeals directly to the Review Commission for contributions; two levels of review for benefits — Board/hierarchical review and the Review Commission). Title Six contains s.229 empowering the provincial Cabinet to designate the tribunal to assume the role of the QPP Review Commission, enabling the PAB to receive jurisdiction in QPP matters (in conjunction with s.87 of the CPP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any analysis must examine the QPP's organization and review scheme because provincial differences (particularly Quebec's) materially affect how the PAB receives and exercises jurisdiction under provincial law, and how procedural routes differ between contributions and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exclusions from PAB jurisdiction (self-employed earnings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 37 of the CPP (and s.193 of the QPP) removes from the PAB's jurisdiction appeals concerning contributions 'in respect... of self-employed earnings'; such appeals fall within the jurisdiction of the income tax/fiscal authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and respect explicit statutory carve-outs when determining whether a matter can be appealed to the PAB; misclassification may lead to jurisdictional error and the wrong forum being invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB's authority to modify its decisions and limits on appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 86 specifies the areas over which the PAB exercises review jurisdiction and defines the authoritativeness of its decisions; it allows the PAB to modify its own decisions and denies the right of appeal in the case of certain decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must note both the PAB's internal corrective powers and statutory limits on further appeals when advising clients or studying remedies — some PAB decisions may be final administratively and only subject to limited judicial review.
